I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Sapporo, Japan at 2026-08-05 08:12 JST (UTC+0900) (2026-08-04T23:12:00Z in UTC), at latitude 43.0618 degrees and longitude 141.3545 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 38.957 degrees and its azimuth is 103.872 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 32.269 degrees and its azimuth is 259.251 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 62.61 percent illuminated, 104.465 degrees from the Sun, and 374216.7 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—you should be able to spot it, assuming the app’s positions are accurate and there are no local obstructions.

The Moon is **32.3° above the horizon**, far enough up to avoid most atmospheric haze, and it is **62.6% illuminated**—a bright, easily visible gibbous Moon. Its angular separation from the Sun is **104.5°**, so it is well away from the Sun in the sky rather than lost in the glare immediately surrounding it. The Sun is at azimuth **103.9°** (east-southeast), while the Moon is at **259.3°** (west-southwest), nearly opposite directions.

Look toward the **west-southwest**, about **32° above the horizon**—roughly one-third of the way from the horizon to overhead. In daylight, the Moon’s low contrast against the blue sky can make it less conspicuous than at night, but a gibbous Moon at that altitude should generally be visible to normal unaided eyesight, especially if you scan slowly around the predicted position. Avoid looking anywhere near the Sun; use the app’s direction only, not the Sun as a visual reference.
